text: Watch the number five. Before the ball arrives, he has already looked both ways.
Two opponents close in. Most midfielders would panic.
He takes one touch — and the pressure is gone. That's Sergio Busquets.
Spain's World Cup-winning coach, Vicente del Bosque, once put it perfectly. If you watch the game, you don't see Busquets. If you watch Busquets, you see the whole game.
He wasn't fast. He didn't score many goals. He rarely did anything that ended up in a highlights video. And yet for fifteen years, he was the player Barcelona and Spain could least afford to lose.
In this video, you'll learn the three habits that made him so hard to press: the scan, the body, and the simple pass.
And for each one, a simple way to practise it — whatever position you play.
Busquets grew up close to the club. His father, Carles, had been a goalkeeper for Barça in the Cruyff years.
In two thousand and eight, Pep Guardiola brought him up from the B team — a tall, thin twenty-year-old almost nobody had heard of. Within months, he was a starter.
Two years later he was a world champion. Then a European champion.
He stayed at Barça for fifteen seasons, and won almost everything there is to win. When he left in twenty twenty-three, the club spent years trying to replace him.
Habit one. The scan.
Busquets looked around constantly. Before every pass came to him, his head turned — over one shoulder, then the other.
Each look answers a question. Where is the pressure coming from? Where is my free teammate?
So by the time the ball reaches him, the decision is already made. He's not reacting to the pressure. He saw it coming two seconds ago.
That's why he so rarely looked rushed. He wasn't faster than everyone else. He was earlier.
The most common mistake is looking only once, too early, and then watching the ball as it travels. By the time it arrives, the picture has changed.
Look as late as you safely can — ideally just before the pass is played to you — and look again if you have time.

Drill: in any passing exercise, ask a teammate to hold up a number of fingers behind you just before passing. You have to shout the number before you receive. It forces you to check your shoulder every single time.
Habit two. The body.
Here's a defensive midfielder receiving with his back to the play. The only pass he can see is the one back to where the ball came from.
Busquets almost never received like that. He stood side-on, half-turned, with his hips open towards the opponent's goal.
From that position he can see the ball, the pressure, and the pitch in front of him — all at once.

And it gives him a trick defenders hated. He could shape his body as if to pass one way, let the presser commit, and then turn the other way with one touch. Often he barely touched the ball at all — he just let it run across his body.
The mistake is getting the angle half-right: standing open, but receiving the ball on the wrong foot. Take it on the foot furthest from the pressure, so your body protects it.

Drill: three players in a triangle. You're in the middle. Every ball you receive must go out to a different player, using no more than two touches, and you're only allowed to receive with the back foot. In ten minutes, your hips will start opening on their own.
Habit three. The simple pass.
When Busquets got the ball, his goal was not to do something spectacular. His goal was to remove the pressure — to get the ball out of the crowded area and to a teammate with time.
One or two touches, a simple pass, and then he moves again — into a new space, ready to receive the next one.
The pass itself is easy. Choosing it is the skill.
Young players often think that the best players are the ones who do the most. Busquets showed the opposite. His value was in doing exactly enough, at exactly the right moment.
The mistake is trying to play the killer pass from deep every time. Usually, the right pass from the pivot is the one that gives a teammate a better version of the same ball.

Drill: play a small-sided game where your team scores a bonus point every time the ball goes from one side of the pitch to the other through the middle player. You'll quickly learn that the simple pass, played early, is the one that opens everything.
One more thing. Busquets was also a brilliant defender — but he rarely made big tackles.
Because he read the game so early, he was usually standing in the passing lane before the pass was played. Opponents simply gave him the ball.
When Barça lost possession, his first job was not to chase. It was to block the pass forward, slow the attack down, and give his teammates time to recover.
The same habit — looking early — makes you a better defender and a better passer at the same time.
So here's your checklist. Scan twice before every ball you receive.
Open your hips, and receive on the foot furthest from the pressure.
Play the pass that helps your team, not the one that impresses the crowd — and then move again.
It will never look spectacular. That's the point. If you do it well, the game will flow through you, and almost nobody will notice why.
